blocks.x: Let's see. Hello. Yeah, you want to tell us your name? My name is Conrad Rodman Jones III. With a capital T. With a capital T. Again, we'll start that way. And this is the first reel.

Well we have switched to the cassette machine there. Let's see if this is working. Yeah. Speaking of the blue horseshoe. Yeah. Connie Jones again. Speaking of the blue horseshoe today. No wait a minute. It's still September the 1st, 1981. Yeah. If my wife is listening I deny it. Okay. But you never said you went there.
Some of your friends told you. In fact I don't even know exactly where it was. It was on the Jefferson Highway, was it?

I never went there either. Other places I went to. But not there. But we're talking about the good old days in Lockport. What day did they have Carnival? It was I think. Could it have been a Tuesday? The Saturday before Mardi Gras. Aha. Yeah that's something I never could figure out. How could Mardi Gras be on a Saturday? Yeah. It was a Saturday before Mardi Gras day. Yeah.

Because most of the people from Lockport would come to New Orleans for Mardi Gras day anyways. Well that makes sense. But it was a while. In fact right after that they started holding it on Fat Tuesday.
Yeah. Did they get many people in from out of town like from Matthews? They had people come from far away. Yeah.
Timedale and all of them. Yeah. It was quite an affair. We had a good time.

Speaking of affairs, I went to Carnival once like that and then we're having Carnival on Sunday. That big day would be Sunday in different towns on the way going down to Grand Isle. But there was nothing on Tuesday on Grand Isle. It was just absolutely a work day. I forget whether the post office was closed or not.
Yeah I found it hard to believe when I moved away from New Orleans. Why didn't people go to work in Philadelphia on Mardi Gras day? I just couldn't understand that.

Yeah. Well, when I was in the Navy, guys would write me from New Orleans and say, Are you coming back for Carnival? It's as though the US Navy would close down for Carnival. Yeah. Okay. Everybody thinks the same way. There was no equivalent in Philadelphia at all.

No. New Year's Day, the Mummers was their Mardi Gras. Held in the dead of winter, snow up to your armpits. And every banjo player for six hundred miles walking down Broad Street freezing to death in these feathered costumes. As many years as I lived in Philadelphia, which was about three, I lived three blocks from where they paraded. I never once saw it. I always watched it on television. It's just too damn cold.
And you never got out your old banjo in March.
Do you know Amy Sharp did not know what the Mummers were? We had to explain it. In fact, she thought we were putting her on for the longest time. Where is she from, Philadelphia?
She's from Forest City, Arkansas.
Oh, yeah.
Oh, yeah. She didn't know what a Mummers band was.

Yeah. You use her how often now? Right now she's working three days a week. While Buzzy was out during the summer with the center stage or whatever it is. She was working six days a week for about two months.
Is she a strong banjo player would you say?

I'll tell you what, she's a good banjo player for what I need as any I've ever had. She's not strong as far as power, sheer power. But then again I don't have a powerful band, I don't have a loud band. But she's one of the best rhythm banjo players that I've ever heard in my life. And how long has she been playing? She's only been playing about three years, totally. She just has that knack, Richard. And the longer she plays the better she will get. She's one of those kind of people who just started late in life. Most people who start that late in life never seem to develop, but she did. She's fortunate. And then Buzzy's something else. Buzzy's a harder player than she is and he's got more technique and a larger repertoire. But then again Buzzy's fifteen years older than she is too.
Well fifteen years old and he's been playing for more than three years. Yeah. And he's been... Probably since he was a kid.

Buzzy started when he was a senior in high school. Amy started when she was a sophomore in college. But Buzzy has the added advantage of having played with your father's mustache bands back when they first started. Which at that time wasn't the hoopla and all the BS that it is. Now they did mostly tunes. They were background music at that time. They did tunes and he learned chord changes and learned how to play rhythm banjo behind a lead banjo player. Now they don't do tunes? Well they do schtick now. They sing alongs and whoopies and hooplas and all that crap. You know it's loud. Get the audience frenzied up and drinking beer and stomping their feet and everything. That's what it developed to a good time whoopie parlor.

I've never have been to one in so many years. See the times I've been to them, although I didn't always like what they were doing, I always respected the musicianship of those players. They were good players.
They had some awfully fine players.
Yeah, I'm talking about the people that say would be playing with Jay Brackett. And of course Les Muscat was working on them.
Jimmy Hazelup. Oh, quite a few good players. Good and agile players.

J.R. Short, is that his name? Do you remember him? No. The trumpet player was named Blood. This may have been when you were in Philadelphia or something. Yeah. J.R. Short is in Detroit I think playing with the new McKinney's Cotton Pickers. He was a tuba player down here in the early 60s now, I don't know where you were then. That's a lot. Yeah, well, there were so many of those bands. He's with the new McKinney Cotton Pickers, isn't he? Yeah. I'm a friend of Dave Wilborn. Oh yeah? How on earth did you know him? From Manassas of all places. He was up there. Jazz Festival. And we got to be buddies. In case whoever's listening to this, he is the last surviving member of the McKinney Cotton Pickers. He was the singer of the band. And he was trying to get the band down here for the New Orleans Jazz and Heritage Festival. But something like that makes too much sense. So they, you know, I don't know.
They didn't bring it down.
Yeah.

In fact I happened to be listening to the band. Yeah. In fact I happened to be listening to the band. He was the band. He was the band. He was the band. He was the band. He was the band. He was trying to get the band down here for the New Orleans Jazz and Heritage Festival. But something like that makes too much sense. So they didn't bring it down.

Yeah. In fact I happened to be listening to that band this morning but on the old McKinney Cotton Pickers, not the new ones. And does Wilburn play an instrument now? No. Wilburn sings. He was a banjo player. Was he? Yeah.

They have two units. They're using a small unit and a large unit. Tommy Saunders is playing trumpet with him sometimes. And Tommy's a wonderful player. And there's some awfully good musicians in the Detroit area too, so I imagine that they can put together some very fine bands. Yeah.
The Gabriel Brothers and their father are up there. Different ones, different New Orleans musicians are up around there too.
I guess the best all around multi-instrumentalist I ever met in my life was from Detroit, went to Wayne State University, Billy Prince. What's his name?
Billy Prince.

He's something else. He's like I said the most unbelievable multi-instrumentalist. You're telling me about him. He was a, his daddy was Grand Prince who wrote a lot of stocks back in the old days. He was a trumpet player with Ben Burnie and all those old-time bands. Yeah there's an awful lot of good players out there. They all have a good symphony orchestra. Yeah.

Well and they have, they had a good reason at one time. I think they've been tearing the Greystone Ballroom down if it's not going I think recently. I don't know. And that was a place that I used to hear people talk about a lot and still do. And of course I never remember there being a big ballroom here in this city like that.

I don't remember either, but then that would, see that would be like slightly before my time. Yeah. When ballrooms were popular. Yeah. I can remember Eddie Miller talking about the Fern Dance Hall. Yeah. And a couple more places if the names don't come to mind right now. And I imagine that maybe they were probably small scale ballrooms. Because it doesn't seem like New Orleans was the kind of town that would have a Roseland or something. No, no. Which is a monstrous thing.

You could dance with broken dishes at the Fern. Broken dishes mean Fawcett's girlfriend. That was not the Greystone Ball. But I absolutely do not ever remember going to a big ballroom except in a hotel. Yeah, all the hotels had ballrooms, but I don't think they were on a steady basis.
It would be like for dances. The Blue Room was going. Yeah, but that's not a ballroom. No. It was a supper club.
No. The Jung had a big room. The Jung had the cotillion. That also was a supper club. Well they had a roof at one time and the Los Radekos had a band there, but I don't recall.
I went to dances at high school proms and things on the roof of the Jung.

Yeah. Yeah, that's the reason I brought it up, because I know your father was associated with the Jung. I crashed a few dances up there. Yeah, you were young and you could get in. Back to that neighborhood, when we left off, I guess it was last time, we were talking about Tony Almarico and how close you lived to him. So when you were a kid did you go to his house?

No, no. I can remember as a kid hearing Tony practice, running scales from scale after scale after scale. That was before I even played trumpet. We'd be, you know, kids played around the neighborhood and everything, I can remember, hearing him play in the afternoon, whether he'd be warming up or just keeping his chops up or between jobs, I don't know. But Tony did not know me from the neighborhood. By the time I started playing in the Parisian Room we had moved out of the neighborhood just a matter of a year or so before that. We had moved out to the lakefront, to Lake Vista, and lived out there. So he didn't know me from the neighborhood, you know, a neighborhood full of kids.
Yeah. But he was an important grown man in your eyes. Oh yes, oh yeah.

Well he had that mystique, he was a musician, a professional musician too. A guy that did it all the time. But we later spoke about, you know, I told him about how I used to listen to him when I was a kid and played. He couldn't even get a kick out of that. Tony was genuinely nice. He was just one of the most giving people that I've ever met in my life. He was just a warm, friendly, just a good man. And he did an awful lot for me and an awful lot for other people too. He's responsible for a lot of people being in the music business today. People who would not necessarily have had the chance to play and be heard. What did you call him? For a long time it was Mr. El Morico. Of course, the days were different in those days. Anyone who was older than you was Mr. and if you grew up with them, I would have had the time to play. And then it became, for some reason, another Nina, which is what? That's Italian. Yeah. I mean, like our nickname.
Yeah. Well, Nina Piconi is really not Nina. Never Tony though, huh? No, not that I can remember. But for a long time it was Mr. El Morico. Of course, the days were different in those days.

Anyone who was older than you was Mr. and if you grew up with them, I would have been a little bit more. And if you grew up with them, it was still Mr. if somebody was 15 years older than you. It was hard making the transition from Mr. Allen to Dick or Richard. Because it just became a habit. Someone was Mr. So and so. And I never did call Jack Teagarden anything but Mr. Teagarden. Now Addie was different, because everybody called her Addie, Mrs. Tebow. But to me, you just didn't speak to a deity on a first name basis.
Who did call him Jack? Everybody. Excuse me, everybody. The first time they ever met him they called him Jack? I don't know.
Yeah, I guess so. Yeah, I think so.
He was that kind of guy.

He was, I mean like when you were talking music and you said Jack, you didn't have to use the last name. Never. Because everybody assumed that it was Jack Teagarden, because that was the most famous Jack in the music business.
Nobody to compare. I've never heard of another Jack.
Not at that level.

Yeah, I mean, not even approaching that level. And I think that's true no matter where you go in this country, if you say Jack. I mean whether you're in Jackson, Mississippi, they might think of Jackson when you say Jackson. That was one of his nicknames. Yeah. He used to call people Jackson.
And Gate. He did, personally. Gate. Gate was another one of his slang endearments.
We've got another ten minutes or so. Okay. Yeah, yeah.
What the hell, I've only got to go to work.
Yeah, well I mean, they don't care. Today's payday, so. Okay, well you get there early. Well, you never heard anybody called Tony pokechop?
Oh yeah, pokechop.
A lot of people did that?

A lot of people did. Roy Zimmerman used to call him pokechops. That was plural, pokechops. Pokechops. Pokechops. As I remember, pokechops. Or pokechops. Maybe it was pokechops. I don't know. Sam Decker Mill called me pokechops.
Hmm. And I've never known why either. It's something I never thought about.

Yeah, I never thought about it either. That was one of his nicknames. He was a, he was just a, I don't know, he was, I don't mean this with any disrespect, but Tony Almerico was what would have been termed, I guess, a square. You know, he was very innocent, very trusting. He didn't, he smoked that cigar. I don't think he probably, in his entire life, never consumed a fifth of alcohol. He wasn't a drinker. And he was a hard worker, and a just getting out and flat hustling kind of guy. And he never expected anybody to ever do it, man. I mean he expected, you know, everybody was the best of everything, and you would, I guess, just have to consider him a square. And I know they used to like to kid him, and they used to play practical jokes on him. He had a thing about having something underfoot. If he was standing up and maybe a matchstick or something was under his shoe, you could tell it, and it made him feel uncomfortable. Yeah. And I can remember Pete telling, he would go on a job and then bring a handful of BBs, and spread it on the bandstands, and keep Porkchop in a state of flat unrest all the time. But I mean they used to play practical jokes on him.
Well if you work with dancers that would be very important, to keep the stage clean.
Oh yeah.

Yeah. I mean, even if you ever worked with any dancers, and what it could do to them. And they could trip and fall, so naturally. That, I never have had the experience of seeing that happen, but I know if I'm emceeing something, and I see something on the stage, I'll kick it out of the way. I'll just, well, famous spitball fights have taken place in the Cab Calloway band, and caused a lot of trouble.
I've been on bands that had fights on stage, but not spitball fights.

Yeah, but, well I mean, the story's about Dizzy Gillespie, ended up stabbing Cab Calloway. Ended up what? Stabbing Cab Calloway. Danny Barker was in the band. Yeah, and he was about, you know, a half an inch or something. No damage or anything. But that's a famous story.
I saw Danny Barker on the street a couple of weeks ago. I hadn't seen him in a long time. Now he's a hell of a storyteller.

Yeah, yeah. Well, anyway, we're getting away from Tony. Did he have dancers then? We talked about him. I can remember. We talked about Lizzy. And of course, Frank would get out and do his act. I don't remember any dances at that time.

Yeah. What was his son-in-law's name? Louis Mitro. D'Amico or something like that. He had a waiter that danced. Joe or something or another. Golly, I'm digging way down deep. He was the doorman at the show bar and is now a dancer. He would go up and work to the freezing room as a waiter on Sunday. And I saw Joe. Joe's got to be my age or maybe a couple of years older. And he went to show bars. And I can remember Joe standing up in front of the 500. Oh, who was the actor and the comedian at the 500? And Joe knew his entire routine. And while he was standing outside, he used to lip sync his routine with this guy. But I think he danced. He would do like a jazz dance because he could do a split with the tray, hold the tray and do the split down to the floor and come back up.
This is a white guy. Yeah. Was it Black Joe who danced? No, no, he was a white guy. And he's still alive you think.
Yeah, oh I saw him a couple of years ago. And he had his little grandson used to dance every once in a while. But I'm trying to think that pork chops and kidney stew come up there.
They may have, but I associate them with Sharky, but they could have been doing it. They could have been working different places.
Yeah, it's confusing. It seems to me that I knew pork chops and kidney stew, but I can't remember now if it was from the Parisian room or from with Sharky's thing.
Or strolling up and down the street. Could have been. From one place to another. And there was a lot of that going on too.
Yeah. Yeah they used to go from club to club.
Yeah, and I tell you, I liked that too. Well back to your neighborhood. You said Johnny Ronica lived out there? Johnny Ronica lived on Canal Street but I didn't know him that well.
I auditioned for his band in the very early 50s, like right after I got out of high school. But I couldn't read well enough to play with his band.
His was a big band?

No, but his was an arranged band. Johnny Ronica is a very fine arranger. And he was playing at Lentz when I auditioned for him. I'm trying to think of who was leaving. Pat Sullivan was a trumpet player. And Pat played no jazz. He played no jazz?
No jazz.

But could read anything. And Pat turned out to be an exceptionally fine lead trumpet player. And he needed somebody to play some jazz. But I couldn't read the book. In those days I couldn't read that well. But that's the first I knew him. And I didn't see Johnny Ronica a few times after that until just a couple of years ago I heard him playing again. I'm trying to think of some of the other musicians that lived in the neighborhood. Sharky lived out in Lake Vista. I thought that was a good piece of it.
Where did you live in Lake Vista? I lived on Snipe Street. And Sharky wasn't far?
No, he wasn't that far away. I'm trying to think of anything. I don't know if it was Thrusher or some street like that he lived on.
They were alphabetical, I still are a judge, on those streets. Birds names. Birds names, were they alphabetical?
I think.
I don't remember. It's been a long time since I've been out there. Well, anyway, damn I hate getting in the middle of stories, but how do you spell Dixie Cats? Your band?
That was D-I-X-I-E-C-A-T-S. Oh no, it was one word. One word? D-I-X-I-E-C-A-T-S.
Yeah. And do you remember the band on your first gig that you went on? Those guys, who they would have been?

Yeah, I can give you a pretty good idea. Probably Eddie Winston on clarinet. We had a guy by the name of Murphy, but I can't remember if that was his first name or his second name. He was a trombone player. Probably Larry Mohobarack on piano. And maybe Charlie Mays on guitar. And Sonny Gammond, Vaughn Gammond Jr. was the drummer. That's probably generally who it was. I don't remember if we had a bass player in those days. Bass fiddle was an awfully hard instrument to find. It wasn't that many people played. Bobby Alexis played with us. But Bobby was, for some reason or another, Bobby wasn't always available. I don't know if he was in, if his school hours were different or what, but he was just about my age. But he later on went up to LSU. His brother was, all three brothers were very good musicians. One of them went to school with Carl Fontana back with Cosmo, what was his name, Cosmo Walters, the head of the band up there at LSU. He was in that band. And then that was Richard Alexis, and then CJ, the next brother, who was a bass player, went out there, and then Bobby went to LSU. So he wasn't around but just a very short time with the band. Bobby played the string bass?
Bobby was a string bass player.
Not brass bass.
No, string bass. Did you hear any banjos or brass basses in those days?

No, they didn't seem to be in style in those days. It was a piano bass drums rhythm section. That was the fad. Now black bands used banjo players. I believe Papa Celestan, Papa Celestan's band played for my senior prom. And he had a banjo in his band. But it was a string bass too. It wasn't a tuba.

The only brass bass player that I can think of that was playing inside then in those days was a guy called Lefty Ironman, who played with Buck Banville at the Plum Plant, the American Legion Dance Hall. That may have been a place you didn't go to.
Now Cink Martin played an iron bass on occasion. He was a good bass player too. Good tuba player. Cink Martin. But not often.
I mean I just didn't hear him do it.
He did a few records. Yeah.
But I mean that's just, I don't remember, when you say it was Sharky in person I don't remember him playing anything but string bass. No I don't either.
But he did a couple of records with Sharky, Over the Waves and things like that, that he played tuba on. He played really good.
You ever get hired for churches? The tape's running out anyway.
Not for church music.
But I mean a church, the churches have dances.
He played St. Dominic's and St. Stephen's, St. Henry's, Sacred Heart, the kid bands.
Primarily for Catholic schools. Yeah. The Catholic churches. Yeah. They would have like CYO dances.
And they would have them on different nights of the week so the kids could go say this night dance hall and this night, keep the kids off the streets. Yeah.

Why don't we call it to a halt? I think the tape's about to run out. And I hate to ask you who your idols were then. And get into the Skunk Hall and the Club Pyramid Ballas. If we've got to talk about them, we ought to talk about them. Skunk Hall and the Pyramid Club.
Yeah. Yeah.
Talk about them at length. Let's run it back and see how it sounds.
